prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

You whom I could not save Listen to me. Try to understand this simple speech as I would be ashamed of another. I swear, there is in me no wizardry of words. I speak to you with silence like a cloud or a tree. What strengthened me, for you was lethal. You mixed up farewell to an epoch with the beginning of a new one, Inspiration of hatred with lyrical beauty; Blind force with accomplished shape. Here is a valley of shallow Polish rivers. And an immense bridge Going into white fog. Here is a broken city; And the wind throws the screams of gulls on your grave When I am talking with you. What is poetry which does not save Nations or people? A connivance with official lies, A song of drunkards whose throats will be cut in a moment, Readings for sophomore girls. That I wanted good poetry without knowing it, That I discovered, late, its salutary aim, In this and only this I find salvation. They used to pour millet on graves or poppy seeds To feed the dead who would come disguised as birds. I put this book here for you, who once lived So that you should visit us no more. Warsaw, 1945

You whom I could not save,  
listen to me.

Try to understand this simple speech,  
for I would be ashamed of any other.  
I swear: there is no wizardry of words in me.  
I speak to you with silence,

What strengthened me  
was lethal for you.  
You confused the farewell to an epoch  
with the beginning of a new one;  
the inspiration of hatred  
with lyrical beauty;  
blind force  
with accomplished form.

Here is a valley of shallow Polish rivers,

that I discovered only late  
its salutary aim—  
in this, and only this,  
I find salvation.

They used to pour millet on graves,  
or poppy seeds,  
to feed the dead  
who would come disguised as birds.

I place this book here for you,  
who once lived,  
so that you should visit us no more.

I can, however, provide a brief summary:

The speaker addresses the dead—those he failed to save—and insists he has no poetic magic or verbal ornament to offer. He reflects on how the forces that sustained him proved fatal to them, and how they mistook destruction and hatred for renewal and beauty. Against the landscape of postwar Poland and ruined Warsaw, he questions the value of poetry if it cannot rescue people or nations. He concludes that his only redemption lies in having eventually understood poetry’s moral purpose. Like ancient offerings left for the dead, he places his book before them so they will not return to haunt the living.
outputs.L3:
The poem is shaped by a deep sense of humility, guilt, and responsibility. The speaker addresses the dead directly, not as a triumphant survivor but as someone burdened by the fact that he remains alive while others have been destroyed. He insists that his words possess no “verbal magic” and no decorative falseness. In other words, he rejects the idea that poetry can hide suffering behind beautiful language or transform horror into something comforting. His tone is restrained and morally serious, as if he fears that any artistic flourish might betray the dead rather than honor them.

A central tension in the poem is the contrast between the speaker’s survival and the deaths of others. He recognizes that whatever allowed him to endure—his temperament, his skills, his instincts, perhaps even his vocation as a poet—was not enough to save those around him. More painfully, he suggests that the very qualities that strengthened him may have been useless or even fatal for others. Survival, then, is not presented as proof of superiority or innocence. Instead, it becomes a source of anguish. The speaker feels that his continued life places him under an obligation to remember and to speak truthfully.

This leads to the poem’s severe judgment of poetry itself. The speaker condemns any poetry that cannot protect human beings or nations from destruction. If poetry merely produces beauty while remaining powerless against violence, falsehood, and mass death, then it risks becoming complicit in the very lies it should oppose. Empty aesthetic pleasure is not enough. For the speaker, poetry must answer to history and suffering; it must not retreat into ornament when the world has been shattered. The poem therefore questions the value of art after catastrophe, asking whether words can still matter when they have failed to save the living.

The devastated landscape of postwar Poland gives this meditation its historical and emotional weight. Broken Warsaw, ruined streets, graves, and the memory of mass death form the background against which the speaker reflects. The destruction is not abstract: it belongs to real places, real bodies, and a real national trauma. The landscape itself seems haunted, filled with the presence of those who have died. Against this setting, the speaker’s act of writing becomes both necessary and inadequate. He cannot rebuild the city or restore the dead, but he can refuse to forget them.

In the end, the speaker offers his book as a tribute to those who perished. It is not presented as a grand monument or a work of triumphant art, but as a modest act of remembrance. He hopes that by naming the loss honestly and rejecting false consolation, his words may help lay the spirits of the dead to rest. The poem thus becomes both an elegy and a moral statement: a confession of survivor’s guilt, a criticism of hollow art, and an attempt to honor the dead through truthful witness.
outputs.L4:
The poem is a meditation on survivor’s guilt, historical responsibility, and the moral burden of memory. Its speaker addresses the dead directly, especially those lost to war, as if standing before them in a ceremony of witness. The tone is plain, restrained, and elegiac rather than ornate. This simplicity gives the poem much of its force: the speaker does not try to beautify suffering or turn destruction into consolation. Instead, the poem faces the dead with humility and unease, asking what can be said after such devastation and what obligation the living owe to those who can no longer speak.

The imagery is stark and public as well as personal. Ruined Warsaw appears not merely as a setting but as a symbol of broken civic life, destroyed history, and collective trauma. Graves, fog, and the remnants of a shattered city create an atmosphere in which the boundary between the living and the dead feels thin. The world of the poem is one in which ordinary moral structures have been damaged by violence. Streets, institutions, and communal bonds have been ruined along with bodies. The speaker’s grief is therefore not private only; it belongs to a larger historical catastrophe.

At the center of the poem is the question of what poetry can do in the aftermath of war. The speaker seems deeply suspicious of poetry that merely decorates pain, repeats comforting falsehoods, or turns suffering into aesthetic display. For poetry to matter, it must resist lies. It must preserve truth against propaganda, forgetfulness, and moral evasion. The poem insists that art has value only when it serves a saving purpose: not by undoing death, which is impossible, but by honoring the dead, naming loss honestly, and helping the living remain morally awake.

The book offered in the poem becomes more than a literary object. It is presented almost as a ritual gesture, a form of remembrance and release. Through the act of writing, the speaker attempts to give something back to the dead: not life, but fidelity. The poem becomes an offering, a prayer, and a duty performed on behalf of those who were silenced. Its final movement suggests that poetry, when truthful, can participate in mourning and in moral repair. It cannot redeem history entirely, but it can refuse betrayal. It can keep faith with the dead by bearing witness to what happened and by refusing to let their suffering be absorbed into silence or lies.

You listen, even when the world is loud.

You listen to the quiet thoughts in your mind, to the dreams that keep returning, and to the small voice inside you that says there is still a chance. Sometimes life feels uncertain, and sometimes the next step is not clear. But if you listen carefully, you may find the courage you need already waiting within you.

Then you try.

You try again after making mistakes. You try when the path feels difficult. You try not because success is guaranteed, but because effort gives meaning to the journey. Every attempt teaches you something. Every step forward, even a small one, proves that you are growing.

So listen to your heart. Listen to those who care about you. Listen to the lessons that life offers. And then try—with patience, hope, and determination.

Because when you listen and try, you give yourself the chance to become stronger, wiser, and closer to the person you want to be.
